# Engineering Question

Every diver knows that pressure increases with depth.

But **how** does pressure change, and why is it the first variable of the entire DiveLab model?

# Learning Objectives

- Distinguish atmospheric, hydrostatic and absolute pressure.
- Compute absolute pressure at depth.
- Explain why pressure is proportional to depth.
- Identify pressure as the input variable for the following chapters.

# 1.1 Why Pressure Matters

Pressure is the first physical quantity that changes when a diver descends. Every phenomenon discussed later—gas compression, buoyancy variation and breathing mechanics—originates from this increase in ambient pressure.

# 1.2 Hydrostatic Pressure

$$
P_{\mathrm{hyd}}=\rho gh
$$

Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth.

# 1.3 Absolute Pressure

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}}=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh
$$

| Depth | Absolute Pressure |
|------:|------------------:|
| 0 m | 1 bar |
| 10 m | 2 bar |
| 20 m | 3 bar |
| 30 m | 4 bar |

::: {.callout-important title="DiveLab Insight"}

Depth does not directly compress gases.

Pressure compresses gases.

:::

# 1.4 Worked Example

At 18 m,

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}}\approx 2.8\ \mathrm{bar}.
$$

# 1.5 Engineering Interpretation

```text
Depth
   ↓
Pressure
```

This is the first transformation of the DiveLab model.

# Chapter Summary

- Pressure increases with depth.
- Hydrostatic pressure is proportional to depth.
- Divers use absolute pressure.
- Pressure is the input to Boyle's Law.

# Key Equations

| Equation | Interpretation |
|:---------|:---------------|
| $P_{\mathrm{hyd}}=\rho gh$ | Hydrostatic pressure |
| $P_{\mathrm{abs}}=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho gh$ | Absolute pressure |

# Exercises

2. Why must Boyle's Law use absolute pressure?
3. Explain the difference between atmospheric and hydrostatic pressure.
